title: Emrys and the Harvest
premise: Ada Brightwater has spent years at Hollow Pines Hospice recording the strange phenomenon she calls the Count: the dying, in their final hours, counting backwards from a number only they seem to know. When her childhood imaginary friend Emrys appears on her porch — unchanged after thirty years, still wearing the same corduroy coat — Ada realizes the Count was never a symptom but an invitation, and that the hospice's newest resident, Mr. Vane, is signing papers that will bind every soul in the valley to whatever waits at zero. As her estranged family converges on the old Brightwater farmhouse for a harvest they don't remember agreeing to, Ada must reconcile loyalty to the people who raised her with the truth she's documented all along: that she was promised to Emrys as a child, and the family knew. To break the contract before Vane signs the last page, Ada must offer the one thing the harvest actually wants — not a life, but the memory of belonging itself.
about_author: Coral Thornbury is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver from rural Vermont whose stories blend domestic dread with folk horror. She writes at dawn, after the last of the dying have finished counting.

chapters.title: The Backwards Prayer
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. On a night shift at Hollow Pines Hospice, Ada records resident Eleanor Marsh counting backwards from 312 in a voice that isn't quite hers. Ada documents it in her leather ledger with ritual precision, treating documentation as prayer. The emotional beat is quiet compulsion — we see a woman who has made order out of something unspeakable, and who suspects, deep down, that her notes are less science than supplication.

chapters.title: Zero at Hollow Pines
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Eleanor reaches zero at 4:17 a.m. and dies smiling, whispering 'thank you for waiting.' The room smells of cut hay though it's November. Ada's colleague Ruth dismisses it; Ada adds a new column to her ledger: what they say at zero. The beat is dread sharpening into purpose — Ada stops being a passive witness and becomes an investigator of her own quiet damnation.

chapters.title: Corduroy
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Arriving home at dawn, Ada finds Emrys on her porch — exactly as she left him at age seven, down to the frayed cuff and the button eyes she swears used to be sewn differently. He says, 'You kept the count going. I'm so proud of you.' She slams the door; his voice continues through the wood. The beat is vertigo: the past arriving punctual, patient, and pleased.

chapters.title: What Mother Signed
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, with a flashback to childhood in italics. Searching her late mother's things for answers about Emrys, Ada finds a 1989 contract in the family Bible — her name on it, her mother's signature below, and a line about 'the Harvest of Names.' The beat is betrayal blooming slowly: the imaginary friend was never imaginary, and the family she loved made a deal with her as collateral.

chapters.title: The Summons Home
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Ada's brother Dale calls: everyone's coming to the farmhouse for 'the harvest,' a tradition none of them can explain agreeing to. His daughter Junie mentions a friend named Emrys who visits her room. Ada realizes the invitation is spreading through the bloodline. The beat is familial unease — a reunion assembling itself like a trap with warm lighting.

chapters.title: Mr. Vane's Papers
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A new hospice resident, Mr. Vane, arrives with no history, no next of kin, and a briefcase of documents he asks staff to witness 'when the time comes.' He counts nothing; instead he hums harvest songs. Ada recognizes the melody from her childhood. The beat is cold recognition: the countdown has an administrator, and he's been waiting for her to notice him.

chapters.title: Junie Counts
chapters.summary: Dale's POV. At the farmhouse, eight-year-old Junie begins counting backwards in her sleep — from 1,000. Dale, terrified and dismissive of Ada's 'nonsense,' tapes paper over the vents. Emrys appears to Junie in daylight, waving from the corn. The beat is paternal denial cracking against evidence a father can't document away.

chapters.title: Ledger of the Dying
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada cross-references thirty years of hospice notes: every person who counted died within the county, and every count ended on a date near the autumn equinox. This year's equinox is six days away. Vane watches her do the math and applauds softly from his doorway. The beat is the horror of pattern — the relief of understanding braided with the terror of what understanding obligates.

chapters.title: Ruth's Number
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ada's skeptical colleague begins counting backwards from 89 during a smoke break, eyes glazed, hay-smell clinging to her scrubs. She begs Ada not to write it down — then begs her to. The beat is guilt and helplessness: Ada's documentation may be the mechanism, her ledger a registry the harvest reads.

chapters.title: Emrys Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada confronts Emrys in the cornfield. He is gentle, funny, achingly familiar — and utterly evasive. He only says: 'You were lonely. I was available. Someone had to hold your name until the season came.' The beat is seduction of comfort: the monster as the kindest presence in Ada's life, which is its own kind of horror.

chapters.title: The Family Bible
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs at the farmhouse. Ada shows Dale and their aunt Wren the 1989 contract. Wren goes white — she witnessed it, thinking it a joke about inheritance. Dale burns it; the ashes arrange themselves into numbers. Junie's count drops to 700. The beat is the family's shared sin surfacing: loyalty to each other built on a lie sold to a child.

chapters.title: Vane's Offer
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Vane reveals the mechanics: the harvest requires a signed relinquishment — someone must give up a name willingly, or the field takes names by force until the quota fills. He offers Ada a pen and a simple trade: her name for the whole valley's safety. The beat is temptation framed as mercy, and Ada's horrifying realization that she's tempted.

chapters.title: Wren's Confession
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren admits the truth: Ada wasn't chosen randomly. Her mother owed a debt from her own childhood — Ada was payment, deferred for thirty years. Wren stayed silent out of love for her sister. The beat is grief without absolution: Ada learns her entire identity was structured around a debt she never incurred.

chapters.title: Six Days
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. With five days left, Ada tries to flee with Junie; the highway loops back to the county line no matter the direction. Emrys sits in the back seat, apologetic: 'It's not a cage, Ada. It's a root system.' The beat is claustrophobic despair — the horror is geographic now, the valley itself a signature.

chapters.title: What the Dying Know
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada returns to the hospice and sits with a counting resident, holding her hand through the final numbers, asking questions between them. The dying woman, at seven, lucid for one moment, whispers: 'Don't give them the name. Give them the remembering. They can't take what's given freely if it costs you everything.' The beat is revelation earned through compassion rather than cleverness.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The family gathers for a last supper they all cook without discussing it, an inherited reflex. Junie counts at 200. Ruth reaches 40. Emrys stands in the yard all night, facing the house, keeping watch — or keeping score. The beat is tender doom: love expressed perfectly inside a structure designed to consume them.

chapters.title: Equinox
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The harvest begins at dawn: the corn moves against the wind, the sky the color of bruised wheat, and every counting voice in the valley synchronizes. Vane sets his papers on the farmhouse table, the final page blank except for a signature line bearing Ada's childhood handwriting already ghosted onto it. The beat is terrible ceremony — the moment the story has been counting toward.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Cornered, Ada picks up the pen — and instead of signing her name, she writes out every memory of Emrys she possesses: the games, the secrets, the feeling of being understood. Giving the remembering freely, as the dying woman instructed. The pages drink the ink. Emrys screams — not in rage, but in hunger denied. The beat is sacrifice as weapon: she destroys the friendship to save the friendless.

chapters.title: Unmade
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Without Ada's memories anchoring him, Emrys unravels into the thing he always was — a hunger wearing affection. Vane's contract voids for lack of consideration; the counts reverse, climbing upward, and the counting residents across the valley wake confused but alive. Ruth reaches 89 again and sobs. The beat is catharsis through loss: victory that feels like amputation.

chapters.title: The Empty Porch
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Days later, Ada stands on her porch where Emrys first returned. She remembers that she had an imaginary friend, but not one detail of him — a smooth absence shaped like a boy. Junie doesn't remember hers either. The beat is bittersweet quiet: the cost paid in full, and the question of whether a self edited is still whole.

chapters.title: New Resident
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A new patient arrives at Hollow Pines: an elderly woman with no history who hums harvest songs and carries a briefcase. She smiles at Ada and says, 'Documentation is a kind of prayer. We heard yours.' Ada opens a fresh ledger and begins writing anyway. The beat is defiance over closure — the cycle may continue, but so will the record.

chapters.title: The Harvest of Names
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Ada's POV, epistolary — excerpts from her new ledger interleaved with present scene. Ada, now training a young nurse, teaches her to document everything, and to ask the dying one question: 'Who held your name?' Some of them smile at that. In the last entry, dated the following equinox, Ada writes: 'Count today: none. Remembering: mine. Belonging: chosen, not assigned.' The beat is hard-won peace — identity rebuilt on truth instead of debt, and vigilance as a form of love.
